title: Machine-readable claim-status vocabulary for the platform's canon-evidence boundary
question: Which existing metadata vocabularies can encode, per statement or per page section, whether a claim on endia.de is an established real-world finding, an engineering-feasibility judgement, a speculative extension, or fictional canon — and how do they interoperate so that one page can carry both its canon anchor and its real-world evidence? Concretely: what do W3C PROV-O (provenance), the W3C Web Annotation Data Model (targeting a specific passage), CiTO (citation typing), schema.org ClaimReview (claim/review markup) and nanopublication assertion models actually represent; where do they fail for mixed fiction/non-fiction content; and which combination would let sibling KUEPER projects and search systems consume the status without treating worldbuilding as evidence? The question is about vocabulary choice and interoperability, not about whether reader-facing labels improve learning.
why_now: README.md defines this repository as the website of a fiction series inside a multi-project ecosystem, and the project's evidence profile is worldbuilding-scientific with an explicit canon/evidence boundary. The repo currently holds only the README and empty external-tasks folders, so no page template or export format exists yet. Choosing the status vocabulary now fixes templates, exports and how sibling projects consume pages; retrofitting it after content exists would touch every page.
real_world_anchor: Semantic-web provenance and annotation standards: W3C PROV-O (Recommendation 2013), W3C Web Annotation Data Model (Recommendation 2017), CiTO, schema.org ClaimReview, and published nanopublication models.
novelty_reason: RES-20261022-DA1793AA covers bibliographic identifiers and citation of the trilogy's volumes and passages (ISBN, ONIX, DNB, DOI) so canon citations survive edition changes; it does not address encoding the epistemic status of a real-world claim. RES-20260903-11C93480 covers reader-facing design guardrails (fiction/fact signalling, source labels) and whether readers learn from fiction; it does not evaluate machine-readable vocabularies or cross-project interoperability. This gap asks which standard can be consumed by search engines and sibling KUEPER tools — a dimension neither prior topic resolves.
